caption: Focus on the color imbalance of the cells.
content:
In the explanation of @g{tips/complete_block/common/parity}{parity}, we saw how parity, such as @b{whether the number of cells is even or odd}, can be important for solving puzzles.
This page introduces an even more powerful concept: the @b{color imbalance} of cells.

content.caption: Color imbalance
content:
We define the @b{color imbalance} as @b{the number of white cells minus the number of black cells}.
For example, the Area below has 8 white cells and 6 black cells, so its color imbalance is 8 - 6 = +2 (2 more white cells).
Likewise, the road below passes through 2 white cells and 3 black cells, so its color imbalance is 2 - 3 = -1 (1 more black cell).

content.caption: Using color imbalance
content: The color imbalance of cells has properties similar to the parity of the number of cells.
For example, for a simple road, reasoning in the same way as with @g{tips/complete_block/road/parity}{the parity of the number of cells} shows that its color imbalance is determined as follows.

items: If both endpoints are white cells @m{true}, the color imbalance is +1.
If both endpoints are black cells @m{false}, the color imbalance is -1.
If the endpoints have different colors, the color imbalance is ±0.

content: Similarly, reasoning about the perimeter of an empty lot in the same way as with @g{tips/complete_block/open/parity}{the parity of the number of cells} shows that its color imbalance is ±0.

Just as with the parity of the number of cells, @b{if the total color imbalance of the terrain does not match the color imbalance of the entire Area, the Area cannot be completely filled}.
The parity of the number of cells is @b{binary}, while color imbalance is @b{an integer}, allowing us to distinguish situations more precisely.

content.caption: Example
content:
Let's continue with Example 2 from the @g{tips/complete_block/common/parity}{page explaining parity}.
The question was whether the Area below could be completely filled with 2-cell blocks.
Looking at the left region, its color imbalance is +2 (@m{true} 12 @m{false} 10).

On the other hand, no matter how a 2-cell block is placed, its color imbalance is ±0 (@m{true} 1 @m{false} 1). Therefore, @b{no matter how many 2-cell blocks are placed, their total color imbalance remains ±0}. Thus, an Area with a color imbalance of +2 cannot be completely filled.

The right region, meanwhile, has a color imbalance of -2 (@m{true} 10 @m{false} 12), so it also cannot be completely filled with 2-cell blocks.
In general, @b{Areas with a large absolute color imbalance tend to be harder to fill}, so it's worth keeping this in mind.
